Abstract. High-performance computing (HPC) has experienced rapid growth in recent years, 
resulting in increased energy consumption and carbon emissions alongside intensifying resource 
demands. The research team has created a model system that analyzes HPC environmental impact 
reduction as part of scenario-based assessments. We examine the energy mix through CIQM-HPC, 
a carbon impact quantification model. The system dynamics' carbon emission growth prediction 
model (HPC-CEGP) enables us to forecast energy requirements and emissions under several 
anticipated growth models. Experts predict that energy consumption will reach 1,200 MWH during 
the year 2030. Using clean energy will expand renewable energy by 8% annually while maintaining 
carbon emissions at 45,000 kg of CO2. The DEIAM model is a dynamic Environmental Impact 
Assessment tool to evaluate cooling water conditions, electronic waste generation, and land 
utilization consequences. HPC tracking lets us determine its environmental impact and shows how 
to anticipate upcoming developments for developing sustainable practices. 
Keywords: HPC; Energy consumption; Resource utilization dynamic model. 
1. Introduction 
In recent years, all substantial computing domains have shown significant growth in high-
performance computing technology, also known as HPC. HPC's critical role extends to advancements 
in artificial intelligence, data science, and cryptocurrency mining. Operating HPC systems requires 
excessive non-renewable power that yields unfavorable environmental consequences. HPC systems 
now operate at swift speeds and consume more energy, generating increased carbon emissions. Fossil 
fuel-derived energy consumption generates additional carbon emissions that build up the greenhouse 
effect. In addition, the increase of HPC has other environmental consequences. Extensive water usage 
in data center cooling operations leads to water wastage and polluted wastewater discharges. 
Replacing equipment parts for high-performance computer clusters will also cause solid waste 
pollution, and e-waste may produce radiation and other problems. HPC facilities also pressure land 
use, potentially harming local ecosystems. HPC centers will also generate noise. Emissions from 
fossil fuel power plants and particulate matter from data centers affect air quality. On a broader scale, 
the infrastructure required for HPC increases environmental costs, which requires a comprehensive 
framework to assess and address the ecological footprint of HPC.

2. Current HPC Energy Consumption and Issues 
2.1 Global HPC Facility Distribution and Scale Overview 
Global HPC energy consumption is widely distributed across various regions, with significant 
differences based on the number of facilities and regional energy infrastructure. The following 
provides a snapshot of the global HPC energy consumption: 
 North America consumes 53,457 GWh of energy across 193 HPC facilities. 
 Europe: 53,006 GWh, spread over 241 facilities, reflecting a high concentration of 
computational resources in both research and private sectors.

This fragmented data shows that while Asia's energy consumption per facility is lower than North

2.2 Capacity Utilization Analysis 
The average utilization rates of HPC systems across different facility types exhibit considerable 
variation, which has direct implications for energy efficiency. Supercomputers have an average 
utilization rate of 60%, reflecting periods of idle time, mainly when demand fluctuates for high-
powered tasks. Cloud-based HPC systems show a higher average utilization of 74%, driven by the 
scalable nature of cloud resources. However, this still indicates significant underuse during off-peak 
hours. University Labs have an average utilization rate of 68%, reflecting the intermittent usage 
typical of academic environments. 
 
Fig. 3 HPC Capacity Utilization Analysis 
In our work, HPC energy use is assumed to scale with the number of active processing units and 
average utilization rates, varying by region and facility type. The energy mix for HPC facilities is 
assumed to reflect regional grid compositions, including both renewable and non-renewable sources. 
The carbon emission coefficient is determined by the standard of energy production, and it varies for 
different energy types. The computing demand for high-performance computing (HPC) will continue 
to grow.

5. Dynamic Environmental Impact Assessment Model (DEIAM) 
5.1 Background of Model Development 
Water Usage and Its Link to Other Key Areas 
In HPC, we mainly use water for cooling because it can absorb much heat without changing the 
temperature. The cooling systems, which need pumps and towers, use more energy. But here's the 
thing - water-cooled systems are quieter than air-cooled ones. Plus, since they depend on water, HPC 
centers tend to be set up where water is plentiful. It means that some areas have better access to 
computing power than others.

6. Conclusion 
This paper comprehensively analyzes the dilemmas associated with environmental issues such as 
energy consumption, water use, and carbon emissions related to high-performance computing 
systems. The Dynamic Environmental Impact Assessment Model (DEIAM) is introduced to provide 
a new framework for quantifying the multi-faceted environmental impact of high-performance 
computing. The key role of renewable energy in reducing carbon emissions is demonstrated by 
incorporating time-related factors and the complex links between water consumption, cooling system 
efficiency, and regional water stress. A 5 percent increase in the share of renewables would reduce 
emissions by about 10 percent across all scenarios, indicating the critical role of policy-driven 
renewable energy integration. The study highlights the environmental interdependencies of HPC, 
such as water-intensive cooling systems that lead to thermal pollution and chemical emissions and 
the life cycle of HPC hardware that leads to e-waste and resource depletion. This model shows how 
water scarcity creates thermal and chemical pollution issues while affecting energy requirements thus 
requiring a complete approach to sustainable HPC systems. The environmental costs of high-
performance computing stand at an important point that requires sustainable management to progress 
forward without endangering Earth's future.  
Energy-efficient cooling systems combined with international e-waste recycling guidelines and 
modular computer structures represent our proposed solution for these problems. The integration of 
innovation methods with environmental management practices enables sustainable ecological 
development and healthful progress through high-performance computing systems. Research 
outcomes shed vital knowledge about the environmental consequences that result from the operation 
of high-performance computing.

Abstract: High-performance computing (HPC) has experienced rapid growth in recent years, resulting in increased energy consumption and carbon emissions alongside intensifying resource demands. The research team has created a model system that analyzes HPC environmental impact reduction as part of scenario-based assessments. We examine the energy mix through CIQM-HPC, a carbon impact quantification model. The system dynamics' carbon emission growth prediction model (HPC-CEGP) enables us to forecast energy requirements and emissions under several anticipated growth models. Experts predict that energy consumption will reach 1,200 MWH during the year 2030. Using clean energy will expand renewable energy by 8% annually while maintaining carbon emissions at 45,000 kg of CO2. The DEIAM model is a dynamic Environmental Impact Assessment tool to evaluate cooling water conditions, electronic waste generation, and land utilization consequences. HPC tracking lets us determine its environmental impact and shows how to anticipate upcoming developments for developing sustainable practices.
